claim: Substance P (SP) modulates pain signaling in vertebrates.
source: Pain signaling in vertebrates is modulated by neuropeptides like Substance P (SP).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information about vertebrate pain signaling.

claim: Tachykinin is required for damage-induced thermal nociceptive sensitization in Drosophila.
source: Tissue-specific knockdowns and genetic mutant analyses revealed that both Tachykinin and Tachykinin-like receptor (DTKR99D) are required for damage-induced thermal nociceptive sensitization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: DTKR99D is required for damage-induced thermal nociceptive sensitization in Drosophila.
source: Tissue-specific knockdowns and genetic mutant analyses revealed that both Tachykinin and Tachykinin-like receptor (DTKR99D) are required for damage-induced thermal nociceptive sensitization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: DTKR99D is required in nociceptive sensory neurons for temperature-dependent increases in firing frequency upon tissue damage.
source: Electrophysiological recording showed that DTKR99D is required in nociceptive sensory neurons for temperature-dependent increases in firing frequency upon tissue damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3.

claim: DTKR overexpression causes behavioral thermal nociceptive hypersensitivity.
source: DTKR overexpression caused both behavioral and electrophysiological thermal nociceptive hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2F.

claim: DTKR overexpression causes electrophysiological thermal nociceptive hypersensitivity.
source: DTKR overexpression caused both behavioral and electrophysiological thermal nociceptive hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3.

claim: Hedgehog is produced by nociceptive sensory neurons following tissue damage.
source: Hedgehog, another key regulator of nociceptive sensitization, was produced by nociceptive sensory neurons following tissue damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6C.

claim: DTKR function is upstream of Hedgehog-dependent sensitization in nociceptive sensory neurons.
source: Surprisingly, genetic epistasis analysis revealed that DTKR function was upstream of Hedgehog-dependent sensitization in nociceptive sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic epistasis experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) regulates nociception in mammals.
source: For example, Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) and Substance P (SP) both regulate nociception in mammals (Harrison and Geppetti, 2001; Seybold, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Substance P (SP) regulates nociception in mammals.
source: For example, Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) and Substance P (SP) both regulate nociception in mammals (Harrison and Geppetti, 2001; Seybold, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nociceptive sensitization can appear as allodynia.
source: This nociceptive sensitization can appear as allodynia - aversive responsiveness to previously innocuous stimuli, or hyperalgesia - exaggerated responsiveness to noxious stimuli (Gold and Gebhart, 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Nociceptive sensitization can appear as hyperalgesia.
source: This nociceptive sensitization can appear as allodynia - aversive responsiveness to previously innocuous stimuli, or hyperalgesia - exaggerated responsiveness to noxious stimuli (Gold and Gebhart, 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SP is highly expressed at the central nerve terminals of nociceptive sensory neurons in mammals.
source: In mammals, SP is highly expressed at the central nerve terminals of nociceptive sensory neurons where it is released as a peptide neurotransmitter (Ribeiro-da-Silva and Hokfelt, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Nociceptive sensory neurons innervate the skin in mammals.
source: These neurons innervate the skin, are activated by noxious environmental stimuli, and project to second order neurons in laminae I of the spinal cord dorsal horn (Allen et al., 1997; Marvizon et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nociceptive sensory neurons are activated by noxious environmental stimuli in mammals.
source: These neurons innervate the skin, are activated by noxious environmental stimuli, and project to second order neurons in laminae I of the spinal cord dorsal horn (Allen et al., 1997; Marvizon et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nociceptive sensory neurons project to second order neurons in laminae I of the spinal cord dorsal horn in mammals.

claim: Spinal neurons express Neurokinin-1 receptor (NK-1R) in mammals.
source: These spinal neurons express a G-Protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), Neurokinin-1 receptor (NK-1R), which binds SP to transmit pain signals to the brain for further processing (Brown et al., 1995; Mantyh et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NK-1R binds SP to transmit pain signals to the brain in mammals.
source: These spinal neurons express a G-Protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), Neurokinin-1 receptor (NK-1R), which binds SP to transmit pain signals to the brain for further processing (Brown et al., 1995; Mantyh et al., 1997).

claim: NK-1R is expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons in mammals.
source: NK-1R is also expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons (Andoh et al., 1996; Li and Zhao, 1998; Segond von Banchet et al., 1999).

claim: SP engagement of NK-1R activates Gqα signaling.
source: Once SP engages NK-1R, Gqα and Gsα signaling are activated leading to increases in intracellular Ca2+ and cAMP (Douglas and Leeman, 2011).

claim: SP engagement of NK-1R activates Gsα signaling.

claim: The Drosophila Tachykinin (dTk) gene encodes a prepro-Tachykinin that is processed into six mature Tachykinin peptides (DTKs).
source: The Drosophila Tachykinin (dTk) gene encodes a prepro-Tachykinin that is processed into six mature Tachykinin peptides (DTKs) (Siviter et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TKR86C shares 32 – 48% identity to mammalian neurokinin receptors.
source: Two Drosophila GPCRs, TKR86C and TKR99D, share 32 – 48% identity to mammalian neurokinin receptors (Li et al., 1991; Monnier et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TKR99D shares 32 – 48% identity to mammalian neurokinin receptors.
source: Two Drosophila GPCRs, TKR86C and TKR99D, share 32 – 48% identity to mammalian neurokinin receptors (Li et al., 1991; Monnier et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All six DTKs can activate TKR99D.
source: All six DTKs and mammalian SP can activate TKR99D, increasing cytoplasmic Ca2+ and cAMP levels (Birse et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian SP can activate TKR99D.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TKR99D activation increases cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels.

claim: TKR99D activation increases cAMP levels.

source: In Drosophila, dTk regulates gut contractions (Siviter et al., 2000), enteroendocrine homeostasis (Amcheslavsky et al., 2014; Song et al., 2014), stress resistance (Kahsai et al., 2010a; Soderberg et al., 2011), olfaction (Ignell et al., 2009), locomotion (Kahsai et al., 2010b), aggressive behaviors (Asahina et al., 2014), and pheromone detection in gustatory neurons (Shankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Noxious thermal stimuli provoke a 360-degree roll along the anterior-posterior body axis in Drosophila larvae.
source: Noxious thermal and mechanical stimuli provoke an aversive withdrawal behavior in larvae: a 360-degree roll along their anterior-posterior body axis (Babcock et al., 2009; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Noxious mechanical stimuli provoke a 360-degree roll along the anterior-posterior body axis in Drosophila larvae.
source: Noxious thermal and mechanical stimuli provoke an aversive withdrawal behavior in larvae: a 360-degree roll along their anterior-posterior body axis (Babcock et al., 2009; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aversive rolling behavior in Drosophila larvae is distinct from normal locomotion.
source: This highly quantifiable behavior is distinct from normal locomotion and light touch responses (Babcock et al., 2009; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aversive rolling behavior in Drosophila larvae is distinct from light touch responses.
source: This highly quantifiable behavior is distinct from normal locomotion and light touch responses (Babcock et al., 2009; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sub-threshold temperature (38°C or below) in Drosophila larvae results in only light touch behaviors.
source: When a larva is challenged with a sub-threshold temperature (38°C or below), only light touch behaviors occur, whereas higher thermal stimuli result in aversive rolling behavior (Babcock et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Higher thermal stimuli result in aversive rolling behavior in Drosophila larvae.
source: When a larva is challenged with a sub-threshold temperature (38°C or below), only light touch behaviors occur, whereas higher thermal stimuli result in aversive rolling behavior (Babcock et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Class IV multi-dendritic neurons innervate the larval barrier epidermis by tiling over it.
source: Peripheral class IV multi-dendritic neurons (class IV neurons) are the nociceptive sensory neurons that innervate the larval barrier epidermis by tiling over it (Gao et al., 1999; Grueber et al., 2003) and mediate the perception of noxious stimuli (Hwang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Class IV multi-dendritic neurons mediate the perception of noxious stimuli in Drosophila larvae.
source: Peripheral class IV multi-dendritic neurons (class IV neurons) are the nociceptive sensory neurons that innervate the larval barrier epidermis by tiling over it (Gao et al., 1999; Grueber et al., 2003) and mediate the perception of noxious stimuli (Hwang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ppk1.9-GAL4 selectively labels class IV nociceptive sensory neurons in the periphery.
source: For genetic manipulations within class IV neurons, ppk1.9-GAL4 has been used widely as the 1.9 kb promoter fragment of pickpocket1 driving Gal4 selectively labels class IV nociceptive sensory neurons in the periphery (Ainsley et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UV light damage to the barrier epidermis causes larvae to display both thermal allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia.
source: When the barrier epidermis is damaged by 254 nm UV light, larvae display both thermal allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia (Babcock et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TNF mediates nociceptive sensitization in Drosophila larvae.
source: Known molecular mediators include but are not limited to cytokines, like TNF (Babcock et al., 2009; Wheeler et al., 2014), neuropeptides, metabolites, ions, and lipids (Gold and Gebhart, 2010; Julius and Basbaum, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling mediates nociceptive sensitization in Drosophila larvae.
source: In addition, Hedgehog (Hh) signaling mediates nociceptive sensitization in Drosophila larvae (Babcock et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Smoothened is required in class IV neurons for thermal allodynia following UV irradiation.
source: The main signal-transducing component of the Hh pathway, smoothened, and its downstream signaling components, such as the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus and a target gene engrailed, are required in class IV neurons for both thermal allodynia and hyperalgesia following UV irradiation (Babcock et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cubitus interruptus is required in class IV neurons for thermal allodynia following UV irradiation.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacologically blocking Smoothened reverses the development of morphine analgesic tolerance in inflammatory pain models in mammals.
source: In mammals, pharmacologically blocking Smoothened reverses the development of morphine analgesic tolerance in inflammatory or neuropathic pain models suggesting that the Smoothened/Hh pathway does regulate analgesia (Babcock et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacologically blocking Smoothened reverses the development of morphine analgesic tolerance in neuropathic pain models in mammals.

claim: Painless mediates baseline thermal nociception in Drosophila larvae.
source: In particular, the Drosophila TRPA family members, Painless (Pain) and TrpA1, mediate baseline thermal nociception in larvae (Babcock et al., 2011; Tracey et al., 2003; Zhong et al., 2012), as well as thermal sensation (Kang et al., 2012) and thermal nociception in adults (Neely et al., 2010).

source: Indeed, direct genetic activation of either the TNF or Hh signaling pathway leads to thermal allodynia that is dependent on Painless.

claim: Direct genetic activation of the Hh signaling pathway leads to thermal allodynia that is dependent on Painless.
source: Indeed, direct genetic activation of either the TNF or Hh signaling pathway leads to thermal allodynia that is dependent on Painless.

claim: Direct genetic activation of Hh leads to TrpA1-dependent thermal hyperalgesia.
source: Direct genetic activation of Hh also leads to TrpA1-dependent thermal hyperalgesia (Babcock et al., 2011).

claim: DTK is not detected in class IV neurons.
source: DTK was not detected in class IV neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Numerous neuronal cell bodies in the larval brain express DTK.
source: Indeed, numerous neuronal cell bodies in the larval brain expressed DTK and these extended tracts into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DTK-expressing neurons in the larval brain extend tracts into the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: Indeed, numerous neuronal cell bodies in the larval brain expressed DTK and these extended tracts into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of UAS-dTkRNAi via Elav(c155)-GAL4 driver decreased DTK expression except for a pair of large descending neuronal cell bodies in the protocerebrum.
source: Expression of a UAS-dTkRNAi transgene via a pan-neuronal Elav(c155)-GAL4 driver decreased DTK expression, except for a pair of large descending neuronal cell bodies in the protocerebrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and their associated projections in the VNC, suggesting that these neurons express an antigen that cross-reacts with the anti-Tachykinin serum.
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A pair of large descending neuronal cell bodies in the protocerebrum express an antigen that cross-reacts with the anti-Tachykinin serum.
source: Expression of a UAS-dTkRNAi transgene via a pan-neuronal Elav(c155)-GAL4 driver decreased DTK expression, except for a pair of large descending neuronal cell bodies in the protocerebrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and their associated projections in the VNC, suggesting that these neurons express an antigen that cross-reacts with the anti-Tachykinin serum.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these neurons remain labeled even after RNAi knockdown of dTk.

claim: Anti-DTK6 labeling in the brain was greatly decreased in homozygous larvae bearing dTkEY21074.
source: Labeling of anti-DTK6 in the brain was also greatly decreased (Figures 1B and C) in homozygous larvae bearing two different dTk alleles, dTkEY21074 and dTkΔ1C,that decrease Tachykinin function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: Anti-DTK6 labeling in the brain was greatly decreased in homozygous larvae bearing dTkΔ1C.
source: Labeling of anti-DTK6 in the brain was also greatly decreased (Figures 1B and C) in homozygous larvae bearing two different dTk alleles, dTkEY21074 and dTkΔ1C,that decrease Tachykinin function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of dTk did not cause baseline nociception defects compared to relevant GAL4 controls.
source: Pan-neuronal knockdown of dTk did not cause baseline nociception defects compared to relevant GAL4 controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Larvae homozygous for dTkEY21074 had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses.
source: Similarly, larvae homozygous or transheterozygous for dTkEY21074 ordTkΔ1C had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Larvae homozygous for dTkΔ1C had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses.
source: Similarly, larvae homozygous or transheterozygous for dTkEY21074 ordTkΔ1C had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Larvae transheterozygous for dTkEY21074 and dTkΔ1C had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses.
source: Similarly, larvae homozygous or transheterozygous for dTkEY21074 ordTkΔ1C had normal baseline thermal nociceptive responses (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Two non-overlapping RNAi transgenes (TkJF01818 and TkKK112227) targeting Tachykinin reduced the allodynia response from 70% to about 20% compared to relevant GAL4 or UAS alone controls 24 hr after UV irradiation.
source: Two non-overlapping RNAi transgenes (TkJF01818 and TkKK112227) targeting Tachykinin reduced the allodynia response from 70% to about 20% compared to relevant GAL4 or UAS alone controls 24 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Class IV-specific knockdown of dTk did not alter thermal allodynia.
source: Consistent with the absence of DTK staining in class IV neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), class IV-specific knockdown of dTk did not alter thermal allodynia (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Heterozygous larvae bearing dTk alleles displayed normal thermal allodynia.
source: Heterozygous larvae bearing these dTk alleles, including a deficiency spanning the dTk locus, displayed normal thermal allodynia (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: All homozygous and transheterozygous combinations of dTk alleles drastically reduced thermal allodynia.
source: By contrast, all homozygous and transheterozygous combinations of dTk alleles drastically reduced thermal allodynia (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Class IV neuron-specific knockdown of dtkr did not lead to defects in baseline nociception.
source: Similar to dTk, no baseline nociception defects were observed upon knockdown of dtkr (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Larvae homozygous for TkR99Df02797 were normal for baseline nociceptive behavior.
source: Larvae homozygous for TkR99Df02797 and TkR99DMB09356 were also normal for baseline nociceptive behavior (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Larvae homozygous for TkR99DMB09356 were normal for baseline nociceptive behavior.
source: Larvae homozygous for TkR99Df02797 and TkR99DMB09356 were also normal for baseline nociceptive behavior (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Class IV neuron-specific expression of UAS-dtkrRNAi significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 or UAS alone controls.
source: Although baseline nociception was unaffected, class IV neuron-specific expression of UAS-dtkrRNAi significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 or UAS alone controls (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of DTKR using a UAS-DTKR-GFP transgene rescued the RNAi-mediated phenotype.
source: This reduction was rescued upon simultaneous overexpression of DTKR using a UAS-DTKR-GFP transgene, suggesting that the RNAi-mediated phenotype was not off-target (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Larvae bearing any homozygous or transheterozygous combination of dtkr alleles displayed greatly reduced thermal allodynia.
source: While all heterozygotes were normal, larvae bearing any homozygous or transheterozygous combination of alleles, including a deficiency spanning the dtkr locus, displayed greatly reduced thermal allodynia (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Restoration of DTKR expression in class IV neurons in a dtkr mutant background fully rescued their allodynia defect.
source: Restoration of DTKR expression in class IV neurons in a dtkr mutant background fully rescued their allodynia defect (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the gene functions in these cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larvae expressing DTKR-GFP within their class IV neurons showed aversive withdrawal to 38°C even in the absence of tissue damage.
source: While GAL4 or UAS alone controls remained non-responsive to sub-threshold 38°C, larvae expressing DTKR-GFP within their class IV neurons showed aversive withdrawal to this temperature even in the absence of tissue damage (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DTKR-GFP localizes to both the neuronal soma and dendritic arbors of class IV neurons.
source: Visualization of the class IV neurons expressing DTKR-GFP showed that the protein localized to both the neuronal soma and dendritic arbors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: DTKR-GFP expression was detected in the VNC, where class IV axonal tracts run immediately adjacent to the axonal projections of the Tachykinin-expressing central neurons.
source: Expression of DTKR-GFP was also detected in the VNC, where class IV axonal tracts run immediately adjacent to the axonal projections of the Tachykinin-expressing central neurons (Figures 2H and I).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging experiments shown in Figures 2H and I.

claim: Mock-treated larvae showed no increase in their firing rates until around 39°C.
source: Mock-treated larvae showed no increase in their firing rates until around 39°C (Figures 3B and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figures 3B and D.

claim: UV-treated larvae showed an increase in firing rate at temperatures from 31°C and higher.
source: However, UV-treated larvae showed an increase in firing rate at temperatures from 31°C and higher (Figures 3C and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: The difference in change in firing rates between UV- and mock-treated larvae was significant between 30°C and 39°C.
source: The difference in change in firing rates between UV- and mock-treated larvae was significant between 30°C and 39°C.
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Class IV neurons of dtkr mutants showed little increase in firing rates even with UV irradiation.
source: Indeed, class IV neurons of dtkr mutants showed little increase in firing rates even with UV irradiation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of dtkr within class IV neurons blocked the UV-induced increase in firing rate.
source: Similarly, knockdown of dtkr within class IV neurons blocked the UV-induced increase in firing rate; UV- and mock-treated UAS-dtkrRNAi-expressing larvae showed no statistically significant difference in firing rate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When DTKR expression was restored only in the class IV neurons in the dtkr mutant background, the firing rates increased with increasing temperature upon UV irradiation.
source: When DTKR expression was restored only in the class IV neurons in the dtkr mutant background, the firing rates increased with increasing temperature upon UV irradiation (Figure 3E and see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for additional control genotypes).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Class IV neurons expressing DTKR-GFP increased their firing rate to thermal stimuli even without UV irradiation.
source: Electrophysiologically, we saw similar results. Class IV neurons expressing DTKR-GFP increased their firing rate to thermal stimuli even without UV irradiation (Figures 3F–H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figures 3F–H.

claim: The magnitude of the increase in firing rate upon DTKR overexpression was comparable to that of UV-treated controls.
source: The magnitude of the increase upon overexpression was comparable to that of UV-treated controls (Figures 3D and H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological experiments shown in Figures 3D and H.

claim: Knockdown of a putative Gαq (CG17760) significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls.
source: Indeed, retesting the strongest hits in greater numbers and analyzing them categorically revealed that knockdown of a putative Gαq (CG17760), Gβ5 (CG10763), and Gγ1 (CG8261) all significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Knockdown of Gβ5 (CG10763) significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls.
source: Indeed, retesting the strongest hits in greater numbers and analyzing them categorically revealed that knockdown of a putative Gαq (CG17760), Gβ5 (CG10763), and Gγ1 (CG8261) all significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Knockdown of Gγ1 (CG8261) significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls.
source: Indeed, retesting the strongest hits in greater numbers and analyzing them categorically revealed that knockdown of a putative Gαq (CG17760), Gβ5 (CG10763), and Gγ1 (CG8261) all significantly reduced thermal allodynia compared to GAL4 and UAS-alone controls (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Expression of UAS-RNAi transgenes targeting CG17760, Gβ5, and Gγ1 blocked the ectopic thermal allodynia induced by DTKR-GFP overexpression.
source: To test if these subunits act downstream of DTKR, we asked whether expression of the relevant UAS-RNAi transgenes could also block the ectopic thermal allodynia induced by DTKR-GFP overexpression (Figure 2F). All of them did (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Double heterozygous combination of dtkr and smo alleles are defective in UV-induced thermal allodynia compared to relevant controls.
source: To determine if Tachykinin signaling genetically interacts with the Hh pathway during thermal allodynia, we tested the behavior of a double heterozygous combination of dtkr and smo alleles. Such larvae are defective in UV-induced thermal allodynia compared to relevant controls (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combining UAS-PtcDN with UAS-dtkrRNAi did not block the ectopic sensitization.
source: For example, to test if Tachykinin signaling is downstream of smo, we combined a dominant negative form of Patched (UAS-PtcDN) that constitutively activates Smo and causes ectopic thermal allodynia (Babcock et al., 2011) with UAS-dtkrRNAi. This did not block the ectopic sensitization (Figure 5C) while a positive control gene downstream of smo did (UAS-engrailedRNAi), suggesting that dtkr does not function downstream of smo.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of Patched (UAS-Ptc) abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP.
source: In a converse experiment, we combined UAS-DTKR-GFP with a number of transgenes capable of interfering with Smo signal transduction. Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of Patched (UAS-Ptc), or a dominant negative form of smo (UAS-smoDN), or a dominant negative form of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (UAS-CiDN), or an RNAi transgene targeting the downstream transcriptional target engrailed (UAS-enRNAi), all abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of a dominant negative form of smo (UAS-smoDN) abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP.
source: In a converse experiment, we combined UAS-DTKR-GFP with a number of transgenes capable of interfering with Smo signal transduction. Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of Patched (UAS-Ptc), or a dominant negative form of smo (UAS-smoDN), or a dominant negative form of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (UAS-CiDN), or an RNAi transgene targeting the downstream transcriptional target engrailed (UAS-enRNAi), all abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of a dominant negative form of Cubitus interruptus (UAS-CiDN) abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP.
source: In a converse experiment, we combined UAS-DTKR-GFP with a number of transgenes capable of interfering with Smo signal transduction. Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of Patched (UAS-Ptc), or a dominant negative form of smo (UAS-smoDN), or a dominant negative form of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (UAS-CiDN), or an RNAi transgene targeting the downstream transcriptional target engrailed (UAS-enRNAi), all abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of Smo signaling via an RNAi transgene targeting engrailed (UAS-enRNAi) abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP.
source: In a converse experiment, we combined UAS-DTKR-GFP with a number of transgenes capable of interfering with Smo signal transduction. Inactivation of Smo signaling via expression of Patched (UAS-Ptc), or a dominant negative form of smo (UAS-smoDN), or a dominant negative form of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (UAS-CiDN), or an RNAi transgene targeting the downstream transcriptional target engrailed (UAS-enRNAi), all abolished the ectopic sensitization induced by overexpression of DTKR-GFP (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DTKR and the TNFR/Wengen signaling pathways function independently of/in parallel to each other during thermal allodynia.
source: We therefore also tested the epistatic relationship between DTKR and the TNFR/Wengen signaling pathways and found that they function independently of/in parallel to each other during thermal allodynia (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combining DTKR overexpression and pain knockdown reduced ectopic thermal allodynia.
source: We formally tested this by combining DTKR overexpression with two non-overlapping UAS-painRNAi transgenes. These UAS-painRNAitransgenes reduced baseline nociception responses to 48°C although not as severely as pain70, a deletion allele of painless (Figure 5—figure supplement 3,4 and . As expected, combining DTKR overexpression and pain knockdown or DTKR and pain70 reduced ectopic thermal allodynia (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Combining DTKR overexpression and pain70 reduced ectopic thermal allodynia.
source: We formally tested this by combining DTKR overexpression with two non-overlapping UAS-painRNAi transgenes. These UAS-painRNAitransgenes reduced baseline nociception responses to 48°C although not as severely as pain70, a deletion allele of painless (Figure 5—figure supplement 3,4 and . As expected, combining DTKR overexpression and pain knockdown or DTKR and pain70 reduced ectopic thermal allodynia (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Overexpression of Hh only in class IV neurons resulted in ectopic sensitization.
source: Thus, we asked if tissue-specific overexpression of UAS-Hh in a variety of tissues could induce ectopic thermal allodynia in the absence of UV. Among class IV neurons, epidermis, and gut, overexpression of Hh only in class IV neurons resulted in ectopic sensitization (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UV irradiation increased intracellular Hh in class IV neurons only incrementally.
source: Mock-treated control neurons did not contain much Hh and UV irradiation increased this basal amount only incrementally (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Combining UV irradiation and expression of UAS-dispRNAi resulted in a drastic increase in intracellular Hh punctae.
source: Knockdown of disp by itself (no UV) had no effect; however combining UV irradiation and expression of UAS-dispRNAi resulted in a drastic increase in intracellular Hh punctae (Figures 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunostaining experiments shown in Figures 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Class IV neuron-specific expression of two non-overlapping UAS-dispRNAi transgenes each reduced UV-induced allodynia.
source: Indeed, class IV neuron-specific expression of two non-overlapping UAS-dispRNAi transgenes each reduced UV-induced allodynia (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of UAS-dispRNAi blocked the ectopic sensitization induced by Hh overexpression.
source: Furthermore, we tested whether expression of UAS-dispRNAi blocked the ectopic sensitization induced by Hh overexpression. It did (Figure 6F), indicating that Disp function is required for production of active Hh in class IV neurons, as in other cell types and that Disp-dependent Hh release is necessary for this genetic allodynia.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of UAS-dispRNAi did not block UAS-TNF-induced ectopic sensitization.
source: disp function was specific; expression of UAS-dispRNAi did not block UAS-TNF-induced ectopic sensitization even though TNF is presumably secreted from class IV neurons in this context (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of UAS-dispRNAi did not block UAS-PtcDN-induced ectopic sensitization.
source: Expression of UAS-dispRNAi did not block UAS-PtcDN-induced ectopic sensitization, suggesting that this does not depend on the generation/presence of active Hh (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: UAS-dispRNAi expression blocked the ectopic sensitization induced by UAS-DTKR-GFP overexpression.
source: Finally, we tested if UAS-dispRNAi expression blocked the ectopic sensitization induced by UAS-DTKR-GFP overexpression. It could, further supporting the idea that Disp-dependent Hh release is downstream of the Tachykinin pathway (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: UV radiation either directly or indirectly activates Tachykinin expression and/or release from peptidergic neuronal projections.
source: We envision that UV radiation either directly or indirectly activates Tachykinin expression and/or release from peptidergic neuronal projections - likely those within the CNS that express DTK and are located near class IV axonal tracts.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Tachykinins diffuse to and ultimately bind DTKR on the plasma membrane of class IV neurons.
source: Following release, we speculate that Tachykinins diffuse to and ultimately bind DTKR on the plasma membrane of class IV neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: One likely downstream consequence of Tachykinin receptor activation is Dispatched-dependent autocrine release of Hh from class IV neurons.
source: One likely downstream consequence of Tachykinin receptor activation is Dispatched-dependent autocrine release of Hh from these neurons.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their genetic epistasis and immunostaining data.

claim: Hh binds to Patched within the same class IV neurons, leading to derepression of Smo and activation of downstream signaling through this pathway.
source: We envision that Hh then binds to Patched within the same class IV neurons, leading to derepression of Smo and activation of downstream signaling through this pathway.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their genetic epistasis data and knowledge of Hh signaling.

claim: Activation of target genes is an essential component of thermal allodynia.
source: One new aspect of the thermal allodynia response dissected here is that the transcription factors Cubitus interruptus and Engrailed act downstream of Smo, suggesting that, as in other Hh-responsive cells (Briscoe and Therond, 2005), activation of target genes is an essential component of thermal allodynia.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data showing that Ci and En are required for thermal allodynia.

claim: Activation of Smo impinges upon Painless through as yet undefined mechanisms to regulate thermal allodynia.
source: Finally, activation of Smo impinges upon Painless through as yet undefined mechanisms to regulate thermal allodynia.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the genetic epistasis data, though the mechanism is unknown.

claim: UV radiation may directly or indirectly trigger Tachykinin expression and/or release from the DTK-expressing neurons.
source: UV radiation may directly or indirectly trigger Tachykinin expression and/or release from the DTK-expressing neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of UV-induced Tachykinin release.

claim: In mammals, UV radiation causes secretion of SP and CGRP from both unmyelinated c fibers and myelinated Aδ fibers nociceptive sensory afferents.
source: Indeed in mammals, UV radiation causes secretion of SP and CGRP from both unmyelinated c fibers and myelinated Aδ fibers nociceptive sensory afferents (Scholzen et al., 1999; Seiffert and Granstein, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the Drosophila intestine Tachykinin release is induced by nutritional and oxidative stress.
source: Furthermore, in the Drosophila intestine Tachykinin release is induced by nutritional and oxidative stress (Soderberg et al., 2011), although the effect of UV has not been examined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: UV causes depolarization and activation of exocytosis of Tachykinin-containing vesicles.
source: The exact mechanism of UV-triggered neuropeptide release remains unclear; however, we speculate that UV causes depolarization and activation of exocytosis of Tachykinin-containing vesicles.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of UV-induced Tachykinin release.

claim: Tachykinin signaling could occur via perisynaptic or volume transmission.
source: Because neuropeptide transmission does not depend on specialized synaptic structures (Zupanc, 1996), we speculate given their proximity that Tachykinin signaling could occur via perisynaptic or volume transmission (Agnati et al., 2006; Nassel, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of Tachykinin signaling, supported by citations about neuropeptide transmission.

claim: Tachykinins may be systemically released into the circulating hemolymph as neurohormones following UV irradiation.
source: An alternative possibility is that Tachykinins are systemically released into the circulating hemolymph (Babcock et al., 2008) as neurohormones (Nassel, 2002) following UV irradiation, either from the neuronal projections near class IV axonal tracts or from others further afield within the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about an alternative mechanism of Tachykinin signaling, supported by citations.

claim: Class IV neurons may be constitutively exposed to a low level of subthreshold DTK peptide in the absence of injury.
source: Indeed the gain-of-function behavioral response induced by overexpression of DTKR, a receptor that has not been reported to have ligand-independent activity (Birse et al., 2006), suggests that class IV neurons may be constitutively exposed to a low level of subthreshold DTK peptide in the absence of injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DTKR overexpression causes sensitization even without injury.

claim: Gq/11 and calcium signaling are both required for acute nociception and nociceptive sensitization.
source: Like most GPCRs, DTKR engages heterotrimeric G proteins to initiate downstream signaling. Gq/11 and calcium signaling are both required for acute nociception and nociceptive sensitization (Tappe-Theodor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DTKR activation leads to an increase in Ca2+, strongly pointing to Gαq as a downstream signaling component.
source: Birse et al. demonstrated that DTKR activation leads to an increase in Ca2+, strongly pointing to Gαq as a downstream signaling component (Birse et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CG17760 is one of three G alpha subunits encoded in the fly genome that has no annotated function in any biological process.
source: To date, CG17760 is one of three G alpha subunits encoded in the fly genome that has no annotated function in any biological process.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the gene.

claim: Gβ5 was one of two G beta subunits with no annotated physiological function.
source: For the G beta and G gamma classes, we identified Gβ5 and Gγ1. Gβ5 was one of two G beta subunits with no annotated physiological function.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the gene.

claim: Gγ1 regulates asymmetric cell division and gastrulation.
source: Gγ1 regulates asymmetric cell division and gastrulation (Izumi et al., 2004), cell division (Yi et al., 2006), wound repair (Lesch et al., 2010), and cell spreading dynamics (Kiger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gγ1 regulates cell division.
source: Gγ1 regulates asymmetric cell division and gastrulation (Izumi et al., 2004), cell division (Yi et al., 2006), wound repair (Lesch et al., 2010), and cell spreading dynamics (Kiger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gγ1 regulates wound repair.
source: Gγ1 regulates asymmetric cell division and gastrulation (Izumi et al., 2004), cell division (Yi et al., 2006), wound repair (Lesch et al., 2010), and cell spreading dynamics (Kiger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gγ1 regulates cell spreading dynamics.
source: Gγ1 regulates asymmetric cell division and gastrulation (Izumi et al., 2004), cell division (Yi et al., 2006), wound repair (Lesch et al., 2010), and cell spreading dynamics (Kiger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TNF and Tachykinin act in parallel or independently during thermal allodynia.
source: All are required for a full thermal allodynia response to UV but genetic epistasis tests reveal that TNF and Tachykinin act in parallel or independently, as do TNF and Hh.
evidence: This is a conclusion from genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TNF and Hh act in parallel or independently during thermal allodynia.
source: All are required for a full thermal allodynia response to UV but genetic epistasis tests reveal that TNF and Tachykinin act in parallel or independently, as do TNF and Hh.
evidence: This is a conclusion from genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Hyperactivation of one pathway (TNF or Tachykinin) may compensate for the lack of the function normally provided by the other parallel pathway following tissue damage.
source: This could suggest that in the genetic epistasis contexts, which rely on class IV neuron-specific pathway activation in the absence of tissue damage, hyperactivation of one pathway (say TNF or Tachykinin) compensates for the lack of the function normally provided by the other parallel pathway following tissue damage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the genetic epistasis results.

claim: Flies transheterozygous for dTk and smo displayed attenuated UV-induced thermal allodynia.
source: First, flies transheterozygous for dTk and smo displayed attenuated UV-induced thermal allodynia.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of canonical downstream Hh signaling components blocks allodynia induced by either UV or Hh hyperactivation.
source: We previously showed that loss of these same components also blocks allodynia induced by either UV or Hh hyperactivation (Babcock et al., 2011), suggesting that these downstream Hh components are also downstream of DTKR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Class IV neurons may need to synthesize their own Hh following a nociceptive stimulus such as UV radiation.
source: The fact that Smo is activated upon overexpression of DTKR within the same cell argues that class IV neurons may need to synthesize their own Hh following a nociceptive stimulus such as UV radiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing that Smo acts downstream of DTKR in the same cells.

claim: Tachykinin signaling leads to Hh expression, Disp-mediated Hh release, or both.
source: Thus, Tachykinin signaling leads to Hh expression, Disp-mediated Hh release, or both (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic and immunostaining data.

claim: Autocrine release of Hh has only been demonstrated in a few non-neuronal contexts to date.
source: Autocrine release of Hh has only been demonstrated in a few non-neuronal contexts to date (Chung and Bunz, 2013; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DTKR is not known to play a patterning role upstream of Smo.
source: This signaling architecture differs from what has been found in Drosophila development in two main ways. One is that DTKR is not known to play a patterning role upstream of Smo.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to known developmental roles of these pathways.

claim: Hh-producing cells are generally not thought to be capable of responding to Hh during the formation of developmental compartment boundaries.
source: The second is that Hh-producing cells are generally not thought to be capable of responding to Hh during the formation of developmental compartment boundaries (Guerrero and Kornberg, 2014; Torroja et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sensitization may involve a simple increase in the expression level of Painless.
source: Because thermal allodynia evoked by UV and Hh-activation requires Ci and En we favor the possibility that sensitization may involve a simple increase in the expression level of Painless, although the above mechanisms are not mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the requirement for transcription factors Ci and En.

claim: Smo activation leads to PKD2L1 recruitment to the primary cilium in fibroblasts, thus regulating local calcium dynamics of this compartment.
source: Altered localization has been observed with a different TRP channel downstream of Hh stimulation; Smo activation leads to PKD2L1 recruitment to the primary cilium in fibroblasts, thus regulating local calcium dynamics of this compartment (Delling et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammals, activation of TRP channels in the periphery leads to release of SP from the nerve termini of primary afferent C fibers in the dorsal horn.
source: In mammals, activation of TRP channels in the periphery leads to release of SP from the nerve termini of primary afferent C fibers in the dorsal horn (Abbadie et al., 1997; Allen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SP and spinal NK-1R have been reported to be required for moderate to intense baseline nociception and inflammatory hyperalgesia in mammals.
source: SP and spinal NK-1R have been reported to be required for moderate to intense baseline nociception and inflammatory hyperalgesia although some discrepancies exist between the pharmacological and genetic knockout data (Cao et al., 1998; De Felipe et al., 1998; Mantyh et al., 1997; Regoli et al., 1994; Woolf et al., 1998; Zimmer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature, though the authors note some discrepancies.

claim: DTK is not expressed in primary nociceptive sensory neurons in Drosophila.
source: The most profound difference of Drosophila Tachykinin signaling anatomically is that DTK is not expressed and does not function in primary nociceptive sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the immunostaining and genetic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DTK does not function in primary nociceptive sensory neurons in Drosophila.
source: The most profound difference of Drosophila Tachykinin signaling anatomically is that DTK is not expressed and does not function in primary nociceptive sensory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DTK is expressed in brain neurons in Drosophila.
source: Rather, DTK is expressed in brain neurons and the larval gut (Siviter et al., 2000), and DTKR functions in class IV neurons to mediate thermal pain sensitization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and immunostaining data in Figure 1.

claim: DTK is expressed in the larval gut in Drosophila.
source: Rather, DTK is expressed in brain neurons and the larval gut (Siviter et al., 2000), and DTKR functions in class IV neurons to mediate thermal pain sensitization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SP could conceivably activate NK-1R in an autocrine fashion in mammals.
source: Indeed, this raises an interesting possibility for mammalian SP studies, because nociceptive sensory neurons themselves express NK-1R (Andoh et al., 1996; Brown et al., 1995; Segond von Banchet et al., 1999) and SP could conceivably activate the receptor in an autocrine fashion.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the expression of NK-1R in nociceptive sensory neurons.

claim: NK-1R in vertebrates might play a sensory neuron-autonomous role in regulating nociception.
source: A testable hypothesis that emerges from our studies is that NK-1R in vertebrates might play a sensory neuron-autonomous role in regulating nociception.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings in Drosophila.

claim: The possibility that NK-1R plays a sensory neuron-autonomous role in regulating nociception has not been adequately tested by genetic analyses in mouse to date.
source: This possibility, while suggested by electrophysiology (Zhang et al., 2007) and expression studies (Andoh et al., 1996; Brown et al., 1995; Segond von Banchet et al., 1999) has not been adequately tested by genetic analyses in mouse to date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature, supported by citations.
